steps: Call emergency services immediately and say: “Suspected stroke.”
Briefly describe the symptoms and say when they started, or when the person was last seen without symptoms.
Do not leave the person alone. Keep them calm, tell them help is coming, and loosen tight clothing.
Watch breathing and consciousness. If the person is unconscious but breathing, place them in the recovery position. Do not raise the upper body of an unconscious person.
If the person stops breathing, start resuscitation (CPR). The dispatcher will guide you.
Unlock the door, turn on lights and gather the person's medication list if possible.
dont: Do not wait to see if the symptoms go away — even if they improve.
Do not give aspirin, blood thinners or any other medication.
Do not give anything to drink or eat (risk of swallowing problems).
Do not let the person drive themselves to hospital.

tell: Where: exact address, floor and how to get in.
Which symptoms: speech, face, arm/leg, vision, dizziness, severe headache.
Since when: time symptoms started, or when the person was last seen without symptoms.
Who is calling: your name and a call-back number. Current medication (especially blood thinners) if known.

stroke.title: Recognize a stroke
stroke.intro: Strokes usually start SUDDENLY. If you notice any of these signs, call emergency services immediately.
stroke.fastIntro: FAST covers the most common warning signs.
stroke.befastIntro: BE-FAST adds Balance and Eyes, which helps recognize more strokes.
stroke.observeA11y: Report {{sign}} sign now. Opens emergency instructions immediately.

B.title: Sudden loss of balance
B.description: Sudden dizziness, loss of balance or coordination, trouble walking.
B.check: Is the person suddenly unsteady, staggering or unable to stand?

E.title: Sudden vision problems
E.description: Sudden loss of vision in one or both eyes, loss of part of the field of vision, or double vision.
E.check: Does the person suddenly see less, see double or lose part of their vision?

F.title: Face drooping
F.description: Sudden drooping or asymmetry of one side of the face.
F.check: Ask the person to smile. Does one side of the face droop?

A.title: Arm weakness
A.description: Sudden weakness, numbness or paralysis of one or both arms.
A.check: Ask the person to raise both arms forward with palms up. Does one arm drift down or not move?

S.title: Speech difficulty
S.description: Sudden slurred speech, difficulty speaking or understanding.
S.check: Ask the person to repeat a simple sentence. Is speech slurred or strange?

T.title: Time to call
T.description: Call emergency services immediately and note the time symptoms started.
T.check: Do not wait. Every minute counts.

stroke.disappearedA11y: Report that the signs went away. Opens emergency instructions.
stroke.notSureBody: If you are unsure or worried, call emergency services. Responders would rather come for nothing than arrive too late.
stroke.noSignsNote: Not seeing these signs does NOT rule out a stroke. Other sudden signs include severe headache, confusion or numbness. If you are worried, call.
otherSigns: Sudden severe headache with no known cause, sometimes with nausea or vomiting
Sudden numbness or paralysis of the face, arm or leg, usually on one side of the body

education.title: About stroke
education.intro: A stroke happens when blood flow to part of the brain is blocked or when a blood vessel in the brain bursts. Brain cells start to die within minutes — fast treatment saves brain tissue.
education.ischemicBody: The most common type. A blood clot blocks an artery supplying the brain. Hospital treatments such as thrombolysis or thrombectomy must be started within hours of symptom onset — which is why calling immediately is essential.
education.hemorrhagicBody: A blood vessel in or around the brain bursts and bleeds. High blood pressure is an important risk factor. It is also a medical emergency.
education.tiaBody: Stroke-like symptoms that go away by themselves, usually within minutes, sometimes after a few hours. A TIA is a warning sign: the risk of a stroke afterwards is high. It is an emergency — call even if you feel fine again.
education.disappearedBody: Only a medical team can tell a TIA from a stroke. Symptoms disappearing does not mean the danger has passed.
education.whyTimeBody: Hospitals can offer treatments that limit brain damage, but many must be started quickly. Knowing when symptoms started helps doctors choose treatment.
education.afterBody: Recovery often involves rehabilitation (physiotherapy, speech therapy, occupational therapy) and treatment of risk factors to prevent another stroke. Support groups can help survivors and families.
education.reviewNotice: Educational content checked against WHO, the German Federal Ministry of Health portal (gesund.bund.de) and the German Stroke Foundation. Not a substitute for medical advice.

nutrition.title: Healthy nutrition
nutrition.body: WHO recommends a balanced diet with at least five servings of fruit and vegetables a day, and less salt, saturated fat and sugar.

activity.title: Physical activity
activity.body: WHO recommends at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity physical activity per week, such as brisk walking. Ask your doctor what is safe for you.

bloodPressure.title: Blood pressure monitoring
bloodPressure.body: High blood pressure often has no symptoms. Have it checked regularly and follow your doctor's advice on home measurement.

smoking.title: Stop smoking
smoking.body: Stopping tobacco use and avoiding second-hand smoke lowers stroke risk. Ask a healthcare professional or a national quit line for support.

alcohol.title: Reduce alcohol
alcohol.body: Limiting alcohol lowers blood pressure and stroke risk. Follow your country's guidelines.

sleep.title: Sleep
sleep.body: Regular, sufficient sleep supports heart health. Loud snoring with breathing pauses should be discussed with a doctor.

diabetes.title: Diabetes management
diabetes.body: Keep regular appointments and follow the management plan agreed with your care team.

followUp.title: Medical follow-up
followUp.body: Regular check-ups help detect risk factors such as high blood pressure or atrial fibrillation early.

adherence.title: Prescribed medication
adherence.body: If you take prescribed medication, take it as agreed with your doctor. Talk to them before changing anything.

symptoms.q: What are the warning signs of stroke?
symptoms.a: WHO lists these sudden warning signs (BE-FAST): Balance – sudden dizziness or loss of balance; Eyes – sudden vision loss; Face – facial droop; Arms – weakness in one or both arms; Speech – slurred or strange speech; Time – call emergency services immediately. A sudden severe headache can also be a sign.

tia.a: A transient ischaemic attack causes stroke-like symptoms that go away, usually within minutes. It is a warning sign that a stroke may follow and is an emergency: call emergency services even if the symptoms have gone.

types.a: Ischemic strokes are caused by a blocked artery and are the most common. Hemorrhagic strokes are caused by bleeding in or around the brain. Both are emergencies.

bloodPressure.a: High blood pressure is one of the most important modifiable risk factors for stroke. It often causes no symptoms, so regular checks are important. Your doctor can tell you what targets apply to you.

atrialFibrillation.a: Atrial fibrillation is an irregular heart rhythm. It can allow clots to form in the heart, which may travel to the brain. People with atrial fibrillation should discuss stroke prevention with their doctor.

prevention.q: How can I lower my stroke risk?
prevention.a: According to WHO, you can lower your risk by controlling high blood pressure, not using tobacco, eating a balanced diet with at least five servings of fruit and vegetables and less salt, being active at least 150 minutes a week, limiting alcohol, and managing diabetes, cholesterol and atrial fibrillation with your doctor.

recovery.a: Recovery often includes rehabilitation such as physiotherapy, speech therapy and occupational therapy. Treating risk factors helps prevent another stroke. Progress can continue for months.

doctorQuestions.q: What should I ask my doctor?
doctorQuestions.a: You could ask: What are my personal risk factors? What blood pressure should I aim for? How often should I be checked? Do I need tests for heart rhythm or cholesterol? What signs mean I should call emergency services?

terms.q: What do neurologist and thrombolysis mean?
terms.a: A neurologist is a doctor specialised in the brain and nerves. Thrombolysis is a hospital treatment that can dissolve some clots in ischemic stroke. Only doctors can decide whether it is suitable, and it must be given quickly.

wait.q: Can I wait to see if symptoms pass?
wait.a: No. Never wait. Possible stroke symptoms are a medical emergency, even if they improve or disappear. Call emergency services immediately.

about.title: About and medical disclaimer
about.mission: A free, international stroke awareness and prevention app to help people recognize the warning signs, react fast and reduce their risk.
about.disclaimer: STROKE GUARD AI provides general health education and emergency orientation. It does not diagnose, detect, rule out or predict a stroke and does not replace a doctor, neurologist or emergency medical service. The app is not a certified medical device and is not clinically validated.
about.review: Medical and emergency content in this version is pending review by qualified medical professionals. Emergency numbers must be verified for each country before publication.
about.free: No advertising, no subscription, no sale of data.
